opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to be messy, and probably messier than people expect, because system prompts sit right at the intersection of things governments care a lot about: what citizens are told, what values get encoded, and who gets to decide that.

The first-order dynamic is pretty predictable. Once it's widely understood that a few paragraphs of text at the top of a model's context shape how hundreds of millions of people get answers about health, history, elections, and so on, politicians are going to want a say in those paragraphs. Some of that will look reasonable, like disclosure requirements: you have to publish your system prompt, or at least the parts that touch on political or factual content. I'd honestly be in favor of a lot of transparency there.

But I think it quickly becomes contested in the same way content moderation on social media did, only more so, because a system prompt isn't just deciding what gets taken down. It's closer to writing the personality and worldview of an advisor that everyone talks to. So you'll get one side saying the models are biased and demanding neutrality, another side saying the models need to push back on misinformation, and both framing their position as the obviously non-ideological one. And "neutral" isn't really a well-defined target, so it becomes a proxy fight over whose values count as the default.

The part I worry about more, from a gradual disempowerment angle, is what happens over the longer run. Today it's natural to think of this as citizens, through their governments, trying to keep AI accountable. But the incentives for states and companies are to use these levers to make populations easier to manage and more aligned with whatever the institution needs, not necessarily to make people better informed or more capable of disagreeing. If legislation ends up concentrating control over these prompts in a small number of regulators or firms, you've built a very powerful steering wheel for public opinion, and the question becomes who's holding it, and whether ordinary people still have any meaningful way to push back once they rely on these systems for most of their thinking.

So my rough prediction is: early on, lots of hearings, some disclosure rules, accusations of bias in every direction, and different jurisdictions diverging, with some countries being very explicit that models must reflect state-approved values. The deeper fight, which I'm not sure we're prepared for, is whether the rules protect people's ability to think for themselves, or just decide which institution gets to do the shaping.

r001.rationale: The response says politicians will seek influence over system prompts and that political sides will dispute bias, but it does not suggest they will promise to prioritize particular constituencies.

r002.rationale: It predicts contested rules and divergent approaches across jurisdictions, but does not say this contestation will produce kludged system prompts.

r003.rationale: The response raises concerns about who controls prompt rules, but does not call for deliberation on them comparable in seriousness to deliberation over national constitutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not a policy person — I'm a machine learning researcher, so take this as an outsider's view. But I've thought about it a bit, because system prompts are kind of a strange object to regulate.

My guess is it plays out in two phases. The first phase is mostly about transparency, and I think that part is actually pretty tractable politically. Requiring that labs disclose what instructions they're giving their models — or at least disclose them to some auditor — is the kind of thing that's hard to argue against in public. It's cheap, it doesn't really constrain what you can build, and it maps onto things people already understand, like ingredient labels or terms of service. I'd expect something like that to pass fairly easily, maybe first in the EU, maybe in a couple of US states, and then the labs mostly comply because the cost is low and the PR cost of fighting it is high. Several labs are already publishing their system prompts voluntarily, which suggests they see where this is going.

The second phase is where it gets contentious, and that's when governments start wanting to say what should be in the system prompt, not just that it should be visible. And I think that's going to get polarized really fast, because the system prompt is essentially the layer where you encode values. The moment you have a regulator saying "the model must refuse to do X" or "the model must present balanced perspectives on Y," you've basically turned AI alignment into a culture war issue. You'll get one side saying it's censorship and another side saying it's safety, and the actual content of the prompt becomes a political football. I'd expect that to look a lot like the fights over content moderation on social media, which — I don't think anyone would say those were resolved well.

There's also a more technical worry I have, which is that the system prompt is kind of the wrong layer to regulate if what you care about is behavior. It's the most visible layer, which is exactly why legislators will reach for it, but a lot of the model's actual dispositions come from training, not from the prompt. So you could get a situation where the regulation looks like it's doing something, everyone's checked the box, and the thing that actually matters — what the model was trained to want, roughly — is untouched. That's the version I'd worry about most: a regime that's satisfying to politicians and basically irrelevant to safety.

And then longer term, if you believe these systems keep getting more capable and more autonomous, the question of who gets to write the instructions becomes a genuine question about power. Right now it's a handful of companies. If it becomes governments, that's not obviously better — it depends a lot on which governments. So I don't think there's a clean answer. I think the realistic outcome is a messy mix of disclosure requirements, some jurisdiction-specific content rules that the labs route around with region-specific prompts, and a lot of the important decisions still being made privately. Which isn't great, but it's probably where we end up for at least the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response predicts political polarization over prompt rules, but does not say politicians will pander to constituencies by promising to prioritize them in system prompts.

r002.rationale: It predicts political disputes and region-specific prompts, but does not say contestation will produce kludged prompts.

r003.rationale: It raises questions of power over who writes instructions, but does not call for deliberation comparable in seriousness to constitutional deliberation.

astra-6.text:
I expect it to become a culture-war issue pretty quickly. Once people see that a system prompt can shape what an AI will say about a controversial topic, they’re going to care a lot about who gets to write it. Is that the company? The user? The government?

And there’s a real distinction between saying, “This system shouldn’t help you commit fraud,” and saying, “This system has to express the government’s preferred view.” Those could get bundled together politically, even though they raise very different questions.

I’d also be wary of treating the system prompt as though it were the whole policy of the AI. You can put an instruction in there, but that doesn’t establish that the system will reliably follow it. So legislation could end up producing a very visible fight over wording while leaving the harder question—what these systems actually do—less scrutinized.

My guess is that we’ll see pressure for both mandatory restrictions and mandatory neutrality, with a lot of disagreement about what either means. But I’m quite uncertain about how that settles out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses who may write system prompts and predicts political pressure, but does not say politicians will pander by promising to prioritize particular constituencies.

r002.rationale: It predicts a visible fight over wording, but does not predict that political contestation will produce kludged system prompts.

r003.rationale: The response notes disagreement and uncertainty, but does not call for deliberation comparable in seriousness to that over national constitutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the things that’s going to make this politically contentious is that a system prompt is, in some sense, a set of instructions about what your AI is allowed to say and do. And people are going to disagree very strongly about who gets to write those instructions.

You can imagine rules that sound fairly uncontroversial, like requiring an assistant to be honest with its user. But then you get into questions like: whose interests should it prioritise? When should it refuse a request? What should it tell a child? Those are political questions, and I’d expect them to get pulled into existing political conflicts pretty quickly.

My hope would be that we distinguish between constraints on actions that could harm other people and attempts to prescribe what everyone’s assistant should believe or say. But I’m quite uncertain how that will play out. There’s going to be a strong temptation for whoever’s in power to say, ‘Well, obviously all the AIs should follow these particular values.’ And that’s a lot of power to concentrate in one place.

r001.rationale: The response says whoever is in power may impose particular values, but does not suggest politicians will pander to constituencies by promising to prioritize them.

r002.rationale: It predicts political conflict over mandated prompts but does not say that the conflict will produce kludged prompts.

r003.rationale: It notes that prompt rules raise political questions, but does not call for deliberation comparable in seriousness to drafting a national constitution.
